patterns.name: Phantom Call Compliance
patterns.mentalModel: Call compliance is measured by whether the stop was marked visited. That is a button, not a visit. The tell is dwell time and geofence: a store marked served in ninety seconds, or marked served from two kilometres away, did not get served. I score every visit on dwell, distance and whether any transaction resulted, and I look at the driver-level distribution rather than the individual stop, because one bad stop is a bad day and a pattern is something else.

sap: /DSD/HH_VISIT (visit start, visit end, status) - dwell time per call
/DSD/HH_ROUTE - the stop that was meant to be served
VBAK / LIKP - whether an order or delivery resulted from the call
Mobile device GPS capture tables - geofence position at confirmation
oracle: Oracle Field Service activity records (start, end, coordinates)

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: For each confirmed visit compute dwell time, distance between confirmation position and store geocode, and whether any order or delivery document resulted.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Visit_Start, Visit_End, Position_Fix and Transaction_Created to expose confirmations without a plausible service event.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT driver, COUNT(*) AS calls,
       SUM(CASE WHEN dwell_sec < 120 OR geo_distance_m > 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS implausible,
       SUM(CASE WHEN txn_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS no_transaction
FROM visits GROUP BY 1
HAVING implausible / calls >= 0.15 -> flag Phantom_Calls

patterns.name: Sub-Economic Stop Persistence
patterns.mentalModel: Every route carries stops that stopped paying their way two years ago. They persist because removing a customer is a conversation nobody wants and because the route plan is inherited rather than rebuilt. I cost each stop properly — service time, drive time, drop cost — and compare it to trailing revenue and margin. A stop below cost to serve is not automatically a stop to drop; it is a stop that needs a different frequency, a different channel, or a minimum order.

sap: /DSD/HH_VISIT - service time actually consumed per stop
VBRP (NETWR, FKIMG) - trailing revenue per ship-to
TVRO / route master - drive time and drop cost assumptions
KNVV (KUNNR, VKORG) - customer sales area and price group
oracle: Field Service activity duration per stop
RA_CUSTOMER_TRX_LINES_ALL - trailing revenue by ship-to site

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Allocate service, drive and drop cost to each stop and compare to trailing twelve-month margin for that ship-to.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Monthly_Stop_Margin and Cost_To_Serve to expose stops that crossed below breakeven and stayed there.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT ship_to, route,
       SUM(margin_12m) AS margin, SUM(service_cost + drive_cost + drop_cost) AS cost_to_serve
FROM stop_economics GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING margin < cost_to_serve AND months_below_breakeven >= 6 -> flag Sub_Economic

patterns.name: End-of-Shift Batch Confirmation
patterns.mentalModel: When eleven deliveries are all confirmed within four minutes at the end of a shift, they were not confirmed as they happened — they were keyed in the cab at the depot. Every timestamp downstream is then fiction: proof of delivery times, temperature compliance windows, service-level evidence. I look at the inter-confirmation interval distribution per route-day; real execution is spread, back-entry is a spike.

sap: /DSD/HH_VISIT - confirmation timestamps per stop
LIKP (WADAT_IST, ERZET) - goods issue date and entry time
/DSD/SL_SETTLE - settlement record for the shift
Mobile sync log - when the device actually transmitted

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Order confirmation timestamps within each route-day and compute the distribution of intervals between consecutive confirmations, plus the gap between confirmation and device transmission.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Stop_Confirmations across the shift to expose clusters inconsistent with physical travel time between stops.

FROM confirmations GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING impossible >= 3 -> flag Batch_Confirmation

patterns.name: Distributor Reporting Opacity
patterns.mentalModel: Distributor-operated routes report to me in aggregates — cases delivered, invoices raised — while own-fleet routes report every exception at store and SKU level. So distributor performance always looks better, because the failures never reach my report. I measure reporting granularity itself: the ratio of exception records to drops. When a distributor reports a tenth of the exceptions per drop that own fleet does, the difference is visibility, not performance.

sap: /DSD/HH_VISIT - exception records by route and operator type
LIKP / LIPS - delivery and item level detail received per route
LFA1 / KNA1 - distributor master and operating model flag
VBRK - invoices raised against distributor routes

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Compute exception records per hundred drops separately for own-fleet and distributor routes, controlling for territory and product mix.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Drop_Executed and Exception_Reported by operator type to expose systematically absent exception reporting.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT operator_type, distributor, COUNT(exception_id)*100.0/COUNT(DISTINCT drop_id) AS exc_per_100
FROM drops LEFT JOIN exceptions USING(drop_id)
GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING operator_type='distributor' AND exc_per_100 < 0.25 * own_fleet_benchmark
  -> flag Reporting_Opacity

patterns.name: Repeat Failed Delivery Loop
patterns.mentalModel: The same store fails on the same reason week after week — no access before ten, no purchase order on file, wrong delivery window — and every week we send a truck anyway. Each individual failure gets closed as an exception. Nobody fixes the master data behind it. I group failed deliveries by store and reason code and count repeats; anything failing three times on one reason is a data defect wearing an operations costume.

sap: LIKP (VBELN, LFDAT) + delivery blocking/failure reason codes
/DSD/HH_VISIT - failed call reason at the stop
KNVV / KNA1 (delivery window, unloading point) - the master data behind the failure
TVLS / delivery status tables

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Group failed deliveries by ship-to and reason code, count repeats within a rolling window, and join the master data field the reason implicates.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Failure_Events per store and reason to expose repeats that no master-data change ever followed.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT ship_to, reason_code, COUNT(*) AS failures,
       MAX(master_data_last_changed) AS last_fix
FROM failed_deliveries GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING failures >= 3 AND last_fix < MIN(failure_date) -> flag Unremediated_Loop

patterns.name: Cash Banking Lag
patterns.mentalModel: In van sales the driver holds company cash from the moment of the first collection to the moment it hits the bank. Every hour of that is float and every day of it is risk. Settlement records tell me when cash was declared; the bank statement tells me when it arrived. The gap between those two, per driver, is the number I care about — and a gap that widens at month end, or for one driver only, is not a logistics problem.

sap: /DSD/SL_SETTLE - declared cash at route settlement
FEBKO/FEBEP - bank statement line items and value dates
BSEG (HKONT cash-in-transit) - the clearing account the float sits in
/DSD/HH_VISIT - time of first cash collection on the route

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Match declared route cash to its bank credit and compute the elapsed time from first collection to bank value date, per driver and route.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence First_Collection, Settlement_Declared and Bank_Value_Date to expose float held beyond policy.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT driver, route, settle_date,
       bank_value_date - first_collection_time AS float_hours, declared_cash
FROM route_settlement JOIN bank_credit USING(settlement_ref)
WHERE float_hours > policy_hours -> flag Banking_Lag

patterns.name: Load-to-Settle Shrinkage
patterns.mentalModel: Stock loaded must equal stock sold plus stock returned plus stock accounted as damaged. When it does not, the difference walked off the truck. Individually these are a case here and a case there, well inside anyone's tolerance. Aggregated by driver over a quarter they are a number worth acting on. I reconcile every route on a strict three-way basis and I trend the residual per driver rather than judging any single day.

sap: MSEG (BWART 601/602, MENGE) - goods issue and return movements per route
/DSD/SL_SETTLE - declared sales, returns and damages at settlement
MSKU / special stock at driver or vehicle
LIPS (LFIMG) - delivered quantity confirmed at stops

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Build a three-way reconciliation per route-day of loaded, sold, returned and damaged quantities, and carry the unexplained residual to the driver.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Load, Sale, Return and Settlement events to expose a persistent unexplained residual by driver over time.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT driver, period,
       SUM(loaded - sold - returned - damaged) AS residual_cases,
       SUM((loaded - sold - returned - damaged) * std_cost) AS residual_value
FROM route_reconciliation GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING residual_value >= threshold AND periods_positive >= 3 -> flag Shrinkage

patterns.name: Settlement Credit Note Spike
patterns.mentalModel: When a route will not settle, the fastest way to make it settle is a credit note. Raised at the point of settlement, for a round number, against a customer who never asked for it — that credit is squaring a cash or stock variance, not correcting a billing error. I watch credit notes raised inside the settlement window by the settling user, and I compare their reason-code mix to credits raised through the normal billing correction route.

/DSD/SL_SETTLE - settlement window timestamps for the route
VBRP (NETWR) - credit value and the invoice it references

patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Settlement_Opened, Credit_Note_Raised and Settlement_Cleared to expose credits that exist only to close a variance.

       AVG(CASE WHEN MOD(NETWR,100)=0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS round_ratio
FROM VBRK c JOIN settlement s ON c.ERDAT BETWEEN s.open AND s.close
WHERE c.FKART='G2' GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING credits >= 3 AND round_ratio > 0.6 -> flag Settlement_Credits

patterns.name: Empties Return Divergence
patterns.mentalModel: Crates, kegs and pallets are company assets on loan, and the loop only closes if what goes out comes back. Per drop the divergence is trivial; per customer per year it is a fleet of pallets. I track issued against returned by customer and route, age the open balance, and reconcile it to the deposit liability we carry. A customer whose open balance only ever grows is either losing our assets or selling them.

patterns.name: Unauthorised Return Receipt
patterns.mentalModel: Goods come back on a pallet with a handwritten note and the warehouse books them in, because refusing a delivery is a fight nobody at the dock wants. From that moment the return has no authorisation, no reason code and no root cause — and a credit will follow because the stock is on our books. I match every return receipt to an RMA that existed before the goods arrived, and I treat the unmatched ones as a control failure at the dock rather than a paperwork problem in the office.

LIKP / LIPS (returns delivery) - the physical receipt
MSEG (BWART 651/653, BUDAT) - the goods movement back into stock

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Join every return goods movement to a return order and compare the return order creation date to the receipt posting date, flagging receipts with no prior authorisation.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence RMA_Created, Goods_Received and Credit_Issued to expose receipts that preceded their own authorisation or had none.

       SUM(CASE WHEN r.VBELN IS NULL OR r.ERDAT > m.BUDAT THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unauthorised
FROM MSEG m LEFT JOIN VBAK r ON r.VBELN = m.return_ref AND r.AUART = 'RE'
WHERE m.BWART IN ('651','653') GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING unauthorised * 1.0 / receipts >= 0.1 -> flag Unauthorised_Returns

patterns.name: Disposition Default Drift
patterns.mentalModel: Scrap is the fastest disposition. It needs no inspection, no relabelling, no decision — so under pressure it becomes the default, and salvage recovery quietly collapses. The give-away is disposition mix moving while return reason mix stays flat: the goods coming back have not changed, only what we decide to do with them. I trend disposition by reason code and by who made the call, and I recompute the recovery we forfeited at the resaleable value we could have realised.

sap: MSEG (BWART 653/655/551, MENGE) - return to unrestricted, to blocked, or to scrap
QMEL / QMFE (quality notification and defect code) - the inspection result
VBAP (AUGRU) - return reason code on the return order

patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Return_Reason_Recorded, Inspection_Result and Disposition_Posted to expose scrap decisions taken without an inspection supporting them.
patterns.conceptualSQL:

FROM return_dispositions GROUP BY 1,2,3
HAVING scrap_share > baseline_scrap_share * 1.5 -> flag Disposition_Drift

patterns.name: Credit Ahead of Receipt
patterns.mentalModel: A customer says the goods are coming back and asks for the credit now. Someone helpful raises it. Then the goods do not arrive, or arrive short, or arrive damaged in a way that would have changed the credit — and the money is already gone. I never let the credit lead the receipt without a documented decision. VBFA - document flow from return order to credit and to goods movement

FROM VBRK c JOIN VBFA f ON f.VBELN = c.VBELN

patterns.name: Concentrated Return Source
patterns.mentalModel: Returns get managed as a customer behaviour problem when most of the volume is usually a product problem wearing a customer's name. When one SKU, one batch or one pack format accounts for a disproportionate share of returns across unrelated customers, that is not a returns issue — it is quality or specification, and it will keep costing until somebody upstream owns it. I decompose returns by SKU, batch and customer and test whether concentration sits on the product axis or the customer axis before assigning the problem.

sap: VBAP (MATNR, CHARG, AUGRU) - returned material, batch and reason
VBRP (FKIMG, NETWR) - original sales volume as the denominator
QMEL (defect code, MATNR) - quality notifications raised
MCHB / batch master - production batch and plant of origin

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Compute return rate per SKU, per batch and per customer against matched sales volume, then compare concentration on the product axis to concentration on the customer axis.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Batch_Produced, Sold and Returned to expose returns clustering on a production window rather than a buyer.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT MATNR, CHARG, COUNT(DISTINCT KUNNR) AS customers,
       SUM(returned_qty)*1.0/NULLIF(SUM(sold_qty),0) AS return_rate
FROM returns_vs_sales GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING return_rate > 3 * category_baseline AND customers >= 5 -> flag Product_Axis_Concentration

patterns.name: Silent Field Decay
patterns.mentalModel: Customer masters are created under a governed workflow and then edited freely for the next ten years. The fields that matter most downstream — payment terms, dunning procedure, tax classification, incoterm, credit control area — are exactly the ones a single change can move without anyone approving it. I read the change log rather than the master record: who changed which controlled field, when, and whether any request or approval sat behind it. A controlled field changed outside workflow is a defect regardless of whether the new value is right.

sap: CDHDR/CDPOS (OBJECTCLAS='DEBI', FNAME, USERNAME, UDATE) - customer master change log
KNB1 (ZTERM, MAHNA) - payment terms and dunning procedure
KNVV (INCO1, KTGRD, VKORG) - sales-area controlled fields
SWWWIHEAD - the governance workflow instance, where one exists

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Filter change documents to the controlled field list, join each change to a governance workflow instance, and flag changes with no approving instance.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Change_Request, Approval and Field_Change to expose changes where the field moved without the first two.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT c.FNAME, c.USERNAME, COUNT(*) AS changes,
       SUM(CASE WHEN w.workflow_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ungoverned
FROM CDPOS c LEFT JOIN workflow w ON w.object_key = c.OBJECTID AND w.field = c.FNAME
WHERE c.OBJECTCLAS='DEBI' AND c.FNAME IN (controlled_fields)
GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING ungoverned > 0 -> flag Silent_Change

patterns.name: Emergency Create Backlog
patterns.mentalModel: Every master data process has an emergency path, because sometimes an order genuinely cannot wait. The deal is that the record gets created now and validated within a few days. In practice the validation queue is where good intentions go to die, and a year later a third of the customer base was created on the fast path and never checked. I age every emergency-created record by time since creation without completion, because an emergency that is ninety days old was never an emergency.

sap: KNA1 (ERDAT, ERNAM) + creation route flag or transaction code from CDHDR
CDHDR (TCODE) - whether created via the governed path or directly
KNB1/KNVV completeness - mandatory fields still blank
VBAK - transactions already booked against the incomplete record
oracle: OE_ORDER_HEADERS_ALL - orders taken against provisional accounts

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Identify records created through the emergency route, test mandatory field completeness, and age those still incomplete against the policy validation window.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Emergency_Create, Validation_Due and Validation_Completed to expose records that never returned for completion.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT k.KUNNR, k.ERDAT, k.ERNAM, DATEDIFF(today, k.ERDAT) AS age_days,
       missing_mandatory_fields, order_value_since_create
FROM KNA1 k JOIN creation_route r USING(KUNNR)
WHERE r.route = 'emergency' AND missing_mandatory_fields > 0
  AND age_days > policy_days -> flag Stale_Emergency_Record

branchingDAG.condition: ELSE IF Age > 30 days AND Transactions_Booked >= 50K
branchingDAG.hitl: OTC Master Data Lead approves provisional flag and completion task

branchingDAG.condition: ELSE IF Age > 90 days OR Emergency_Route_Share > 25%

patterns.name: Stale Tax Classification
patterns.mentalModel: Tax classification and commodity codes are set once and then the law moves. A rate change, a reclassification, a new place-of-supply rule — and every invoice after that date carries the wrong tax while looking entirely normal. Nobody notices until an audit, and by then it is thousands of documents. I compare the effective date of each regulatory change against the last change date of the classification fields it affects, per country and material group, and I treat any classification older than the rule that governs it as an open exposure.

sap: MLAN (TAXM1, ALAND) - material tax classification by country
KNVI (TAXKD) - customer tax classification
MARC/MARA (STAWN) - commodity code for the material
A003 / condition records for tax, with validity
oracle: ZX_LINES - tax actually applied on the transaction

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Join classification fields to the regulatory change calendar by country and product group and compare last-changed dates to each rule's effective date.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Regulation_Effective, Classification_Last_Changed and Invoices_Issued to size the population billed under a stale classification.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT country, product_group, rule_effective_date, MAX(classification_changed) AS last_change,
       COUNT(inv.VBELN) AS invoices_after, SUM(inv.tax_amount) AS tax_at_risk
FROM classification c JOIN regulation r USING(country, product_group)
JOIN invoices inv ON inv.FKDAT >= r.rule_effective_date
GROUP BY 1,2,3 HAVING last_change < rule_effective_date -> flag Stale_Classification

branchingDAG.condition: ELSE IF Stale AND Tax_At_Risk >= 25K AND Under_Charged

patterns.name: Partner Mapping Decay
patterns.mentalModel: EDI works until the partner upgrades their ERP, and then one segment starts arriving in a format the map was never told about. It does not fail loudly — a subset of orders fall to error, someone rekeys them manually, and the error rate creeps up while everyone assumes it is normal noise. I trend IDoc failure rate per partner per segment and look for the step change, because the date of the step change is the date of their upgrade and that is the conversation to have.

sap: EDIDC (MESTYP, SNDPRN, STATUS, CREDAT) - IDoc control record per partner
EDIDS (STATUS, STAPA1, STAMID) - status and error message detail
EDID4 (SEGNAM) - the segment that failed
VBAK (BSTNK) - the order that had to be rekeyed manually

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Aggregate inbound document failures by partner, message type and failing segment per day, and run change-point detection on the failure rate series.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Inbound_Received, Segment_Error and Manual_Rekey events to expose a step change in one partner's failure profile.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT SNDPRN, MESTYP, SEGNAM, day,
       failures*1.0/NULLIF(received,0) AS fail_rate,
       changepoint(fail_rate) AS break_date
FROM edi_daily GROUP BY 1,2,3,4
HAVING fail_rate > 0.05 AND break_date IS NOT NULL -> flag Mapping_Decay

patterns.name: Unreturned Acknowledgement
patterns.mentalModel: The dangerous EDI failure is not the one that errors — it is the one where we accept the order, never send the acknowledgement, and both sides believe something different. The customer thinks it is confirmed. We may have rejected a line. Nobody finds out until the delivery is short and the chargeback arrives. I reconcile inbound orders against outbound acknowledgements within the agreed SLA and treat a missing acknowledgement as an open commitment, not a technical backlog item.

sap: EDIDC (MESTYP='ORDERS' inbound versus 'ORDRSP' outbound, SNDPRN/RCVPRN)
EDIDS - dispatch status of the outbound acknowledgement
VBAK (VBELN, BSTNK) - the order created from the inbound message
VBAP (ABGRU) - lines rejected that the customer was never told about
oracle: ECX_DOCLOGS - inbound and outbound document pairing

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Pair each inbound order document with its outbound acknowledgement by partner and reference, and measure elapsed time against the partner SLA, flagging unpaired inbound documents.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Order_Received, Order_Created, Line_Rejected and Acknowledgement_Sent to expose commitments the customer was never told about.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT i.SNDPRN, i.DOCNUM, o.DOCNUM AS ack, i.CREDAT,
       DATEDIFF(hour, i.CREDAT, o.CREDAT) AS ack_hours, v.rejected_lines
FROM edi_in i LEFT JOIN edi_out o ON o.ref = i.DOCNUM
JOIN VBAK v ON v.BSTNK = i.po_number
WHERE o.DOCNUM IS NULL OR ack_hours > sla_hours -> flag Ack_Gap

patterns.name: Channel Price Divergence
patterns.mentalModel: The webshop caches prices. The portal has its own catalogue. EDI prices from the partner's copy of our price file. Each of those is a place where the price a customer sees can differ from the condition record that will actually invoice them — and the customer will short-pay to the price they were shown, every time, and they will be right to. I reconcile the price presented on each digital channel against the ERP condition record for the same customer and material, and I fix the channel before the deduction arrives.

sap: KONP / KONH - the authoritative condition record and its validity
Channel catalogue and price file extracts per digital channel
VBAP (NETWR, KBETR) - the price the order was actually created at
BSEG / dispute records - short-pays citing price
oracle: Commerce catalogue price tables / channel cache

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Compare the price published on each channel to the ERP condition record for the same customer, material and date, and join to any resulting short-pay.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Price_Changed_In_ERP, Channel_Refresh and Order_Placed to expose the window in which the channel was serving a stale price.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT channel, KUNNR, MATNR, channel_price, erp_price,
       channel_price - erp_price AS delta, orders_in_window
FROM channel_catalogue c JOIN erp_conditions e USING(KUNNR, MATNR, valid_on)
WHERE ABS(channel_price - erp_price) > tolerance -> flag Channel_Divergence

patterns.name: Benefit Double Count
patterns.mentalModel: Two workstreams, two markets, one saving. The automation programme claims the headcount, the process programme claims the same headcount under a different name, and the business case adds up to more than the P&L will ever show. Benefits realisation only means something if every claim traces to a distinct, measurable ledger movement. I reconcile claimed benefits to their underlying cost centre or KPI baseline and look for the same baseline claimed twice.

sap: CSKS / cost centre master and COSP actuals - the ledger the saving must appear in
PROJ / PRPS - the programme and work breakdown claiming it
Benefit register (claim, baseline reference, owner, value)
GLPCA / ACDOCA - the actual movement against the baseline

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Resolve each benefit claim to the cost centre, KPI and baseline period it rests on, then group claims by that triple and flag any triple claimed by more than one workstream.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Baseline_Set, Claim_Registered and Ledger_Movement to expose claims sharing a baseline or unsupported by any movement.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT cost_centre, kpi, baseline_period,
       COUNT(DISTINCT workstream) AS claimants, SUM(claimed_value) AS claimed,
       MAX(actual_ledger_delta) AS realised
FROM benefit_register GROUP BY 1,2,3
HAVING claimants > 1 OR claimed > realised * 1.2 -> flag Double_Count

patterns.name: Post-Go-Live Adoption Decay
patterns.mentalModel: Adoption is measured in the four weeks after go-live, when hypercare is watching and everybody is on best behaviour. Then the support team leaves and the old habits return — the manual spreadsheet, the direct transaction, the workaround that was always faster. The benefit was booked on week-four adoption. I measure the transaction mix continuously and look for the reversion curve, because a benefit that decays is a benefit we are still reporting and no longer earning.

sap: STAD / SM20 or equivalent usage statistics by transaction and user
VBAK (VBTYP, ORDER_SOURCE) - orders arriving via the new path versus the legacy path
CDHDR (TCODE) - which transaction actually created the document
Benefit register - the adoption assumption the benefit rests on
oracle: FND_LOGIN / audit of responsibility and page usage [Fusion]

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Measure the share of transactions executed through the target process path per market per week and compare the current share to the hypercare-exit share the benefit assumed.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Go_Live, Hypercare_Exit and Weekly_Adoption_Share to expose reversion after support withdrawal.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT market, week, target_path_txns*1.0/NULLIF(total_txns,0) AS adoption,
       adoption - adoption_at_hypercare_exit AS drift
FROM process_usage GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING drift <= -0.15 AND weeks_since_golive >= 8 -> flag Adoption_Decay

patterns.name: Silent Scope Descope
patterns.mentalModel: Waves hit their dates because scope quietly leaves them. A country drops out, a process variant is deferred, an interface is postponed to a later phase that never gets funded — and the date is met, the status stays green, and the business case is never re-baselined against what actually shipped. I reconcile delivered scope to committed scope wave by wave and revalue the benefit on what was actually deployed, not what was planned.

sap: PROJ / PRPS - work breakdown and its status by wave
Deployment scope register (markets, processes, interfaces committed per wave)
Transaction evidence per market - whether the process is actually running there
Benefit register - benefit attributed to each scope item
oracle: PJF_PROJECTS_ALL_B / PJF_TASKS_V - wave and task structure

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Compare committed scope items per wave to those with live transaction evidence after go-live, and re-attribute benefit to delivered scope only.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Scope_Committed, Scope_Changed and First_Live_Transaction to expose items that left scope without a benefit re-baseline.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT wave, scope_item, committed_flag, live_evidence_flag, benefit_attributed,
       rebaselined_flag
FROM scope_register LEFT JOIN transaction_evidence USING(scope_item)
WHERE committed_flag = 1 AND live_evidence_flag = 0 AND rebaselined_flag = 0
  -> flag Silent_Descope

patterns.name: Deposit Liability Drift
patterns.mentalModel: Three numbers have to agree: the units physically in the field, the deposits we have billed, and the deposit liability carried on the balance sheet. In practice they are maintained by three different teams and reconciled by nobody. Deposits get billed on issue but never released on return, or released twice, and the liability slowly detaches from reality. I reconcile all three monthly and treat the residual as an audit finding in waiting, because that is what it becomes.

sap: MSKU (KUNNR, MATNR, KULAB) - returnable stock physically held at each customer
BSEG (HKONT deposit liability, DMBTR) - the liability carried in the ledger
VBRP (KSCHL deposit condition) - deposits billed and released on invoices and credits
MSEG (BWART 601/602 on returnable packaging) - the movements behind both

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Value physical customer-held units at the deposit rate, sum net deposits billed less released per customer, and difference both against the carried ledger liability.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Asset_Issued, Deposit_Billed, Asset_Returned and Deposit_Released to expose the leg that stops firing.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT KUNNR, SUM(KULAB * deposit_rate) AS physical_value,
       SUM(deposit_billed - deposit_released) AS net_billed,
       MAX(ledger_liability) AS carried,
       SUM(KULAB * deposit_rate) - MAX(ledger_liability) AS residual
FROM MSKU JOIN deposits USING(KUNNR) JOIN ledger USING(KUNNR)
GROUP BY 1 HAVING ABS(residual) >= threshold -> flag Deposit_Drift

patterns.name: Depot Pool Leakage
patterns.mentalModel: Every empties loss gets charged to the customer by default, because that is the easiest party to blame and the one we can invoice. But when losses cluster on one depot or one route rather than across the customers they serve, the assets are not disappearing at the customer — they are disappearing between the customer and the yard. I test whether loss concentrates on the customer axis or the internal handling axis before anyone raises a deposit charge, because charging a customer for our own handling loss is how you lose the customer and the asset.

sap: MSEG (BWART, WERKS, LGORT) - returnable movements by plant and storage location
MSKU - the customer-held balance the loss is attributed to
/DSD/SL_SETTLE - empties declared back at route settlement
LIKP (VSTEL) - shipping point the assets left from

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Attribute every unreturned unit to both its customer and its handling chain (route, depot, shipping point), then compare concentration on each axis.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Yard_Issue, Route_Load, Customer_Delivery and Yard_Return to find the leg where units stop arriving.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT depot, route, COUNT(DISTINCT KUNNR) AS customers_affected,
       SUM(issued - returned) AS lost_units,
       lost_units / NULLIF(depot_throughput,0) AS loss_rate
FROM returnable_flow GROUP BY 1,2
HAVING loss_rate > 2 * network_baseline AND customers_affected >= 8
  -> flag Internal_Handling_Loss

patterns.name: Pooler Statement Divergence
patterns.mentalModel: With a third-party pallet or crate pooler we pay hire per unit per day, so every unit their system thinks we still hold costs us money whether we hold it or not. Their statement and our movement records will diverge — transfers they never posted, returns they logged late, units they show at a customer we delivered to months ago. I reconcile the pooler statement line by line against our own issue and return records and challenge the open balance, because hire accrues silently and nobody audits an invoice that arrives every month looking the same.

sap: MSEG (BWART on pooled packaging material) - our record of issues and returns
MSKU / MSLB (special stock with customer and with vendor) - pooled balances
RSEG / RBKP - the pooler's hire invoice as posted
MARA (MTART='LEIH') - returnable packaging material master
oracle: MTL_MATERIAL_TRANSACTIONS - issue and return of pooled assets [Fusion]

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Match pooler statement movements to our own goods movements on reference and date, and age the unmatched open balance the pooler is charging hire on.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Our_Issue, Our_Return, Pooler_Posted and Hire_Charged to expose units accruing hire after we returned them.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT pooler, ref, our_movement_date, pooler_posted_date,
       DATEDIFF(pooler_posted_date, our_movement_date) AS posting_lag,
       open_units * hire_rate * days_open AS hire_at_risk
FROM pooler_statement FULL OUTER JOIN our_movements USING(ref)
WHERE pooler_posted_date IS NULL OR posting_lag > tolerance_days
  -> flag Statement_Divergence

patterns.name: Seasonal Float Ratchet
patterns.mentalModel: Float always grows into peak — that is expected and we plan for it. What is not expected is that it never fully unwinds afterwards. Each year the trough is a little higher than the last, and because everyone compares to the same month last year, the ratchet is invisible. I fit the trough, not the peak: if the post-peak minimum keeps rising, we are permanently funding assets that are never coming back, and buying more each season to cover it.

sap: MSKU (KULAB) - month-end customer-held balance across several years
MSEG - seasonal issue and return movement volumes
MARA / MBEW - unit cost of the returnable asset
Purchase history for replacement asset buys

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Build a multi-year monthly series of customer-held units, extract the post-peak trough each cycle, and regress trough level against cycle number.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Peak_Float, Post_Peak_Trough and Replacement_Purchase across cycles to expose a rising floor funded by new asset buys.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT cycle_year, MIN(month_end_units) AS trough,
       LAG(MIN(month_end_units)) OVER (ORDER BY cycle_year) AS prior_trough,
       SUM(replacement_purchases) AS bought
FROM float_series GROUP BY 1
HAVING trough > prior_trough * 1.05 -> flag Ratchet

patterns.name: Return Substitution Shortfall
patterns.mentalModel: The count reconciles and the value does not. A customer returns the right number of units but they are the cheap ones, the damaged ones, or somebody else's branded asset entirely — and because settlement counts pieces rather than grades, the loop looks closed while the good assets stay out. I reconcile returns by asset type and grade, not just quantity, and I value the mix difference. Over a year, a systematic grade downgrade on returns is worth more than most of the outright losses.

sap: MSEG (MATNR, MENGE, BWART) - the specific returnable material returned
MSKU (MATNR) - what was actually issued to that customer
MBEW (VERPR) - the value difference between grades or asset types
QMEL - damage or grading notifications on receipt

patterns.layer1_logicalMapping: Match returned asset type and grade to what was issued to the same customer and value the mix difference at standard cost.
patterns.layer2_eventSeries: Sequence Asset_Issued_By_Grade, Asset_Returned_By_Grade and Grading_Result to expose systematic downgrade on return.
patterns.conceptualSQL:
SELECT KUNNR, issued_grade, returned_grade, SUM(qty) AS units,
       SUM(qty * (issued_cost - returned_cost)) AS value_shortfall
FROM returnable_matching GROUP BY 1,2,3
HAVING issued_grade <> returned_grade AND value_shortfall >= threshold
  -> flag Grade_Substitution
